item.title: When The Nervous System Is Listening: How Trauma Shapes Communication, Interpretation, and Connection
item.description:
Too often we don’t listen with our ears alone; sometimes our history is listening, too. Having a history of trauma can affect you in more ways than just your memories, emotions, relationships, personality, and inability to move on. One of the ways that trauma will affect your relationships is through communication.

How Communication Works

Communication is not just received through our ears by the direct words of another person. It is filtered through our nervous system, past experiences, trauma, expectations for safety, potential threats, and meanings.

This includes hidden agendas, perceptions, as well as the meanings a person has learned to attach to the words being said by another person, such as their tone, facial expressions, and behaviors. Non-verbal communication is about 90% of all our communication, and it is read through our past experiences, most notably our trauma as interpreted by our nervous system.

Trauma affects not only what a person communicates to others, but it is also impacted by what their nervous system permits them to hear, interpret, retain, and respond to. The trauma suddenly becomes the filter that everything is passed through. A trauma survivor will often receive a different message from the one that is being sent, but it also interprets the intention behind it.

For example, have you ever played the game of telephone? A message is whispered from one to another and then translated to the next person repeatedly until it reaches the last one in the room. What’s left is a message that is nothing like the original that was stated.

This is a prime example of how communication is both translated, filtered, and received differently from one person to another based on a multitude of factors, most significantly the trauma filters involved in receiving communications. Those filters can include fears of rejection, abandonment, being held responsible/blamed, being a burden, feelings of worthlessness, etc.

Trauma and Communication

In all communication, there is a difference between what has been said and what has been received. This includes the speaker’s intent, delivery, and the receiver’s interpretation. Trauma can result in widening the distance between the two. For instance, your partner may say, “We need to talk.”

Their intent may be: “I’m concerned about you,” “You seem to not be yourself,” or “I know you’re hurting.” What you, as the trauma-affected receiver, hear is: “I’m in trouble, it’s my fault, you’re going to leave me, I’m a burden, I’m an embarrassment, I’m always the problem.” The interpretations don’t change the literal words that are said, but the meaning assigned to them becomes completely different.

When shame is listening, correction can sound like condemnation. Often one of the primary trauma filters that is in place is shame. Once shame enters the conversation, the person may defend against a perceived attack on identity rather than respond to the actual concern. Shame becomes a significant factor in any trauma because shame attacks our character.

Shame says, “If I did something bad or something bad was done to me, I am bad.” Shame then becomes the filter through which all communication is sifted, and it clouds the interpretation of what has been said and what has been received. Much of what will be discussed throughout this article can be blamed on that shame filter distorting what is heard.

When shame attacks character, any communication that is filtered through it becomes an arrow that delivers more confirmation of that shame. Some of the previous examples were: “It’s my fault,” “I’m a burden,” “I’m always the problem,” which are all received through a lens of shame that reinforces that you are bad.

Trauma and the Brain

Trauma affects our feelings of safety and causes us to doubt our ability to detect and determine threats. Trauma does substantial damage to our threat-detection system and increases the size of our amygdala, causing it to fire rapidly and be on high alert to potential threats.

The amygdala is where your fight/flight/freeze response is enacted; your emotions become highly reactive, and your brain’s alarm system goes into overdrive, telling you everything is a threat. The prefrontal cortex is where your logic and reasoning power reside, and it sends signals to your amygdala, telling it there is no reason to be alarmed.

Before the trauma, your prefrontal cortex was able to send logic to your alarm system in the amygdala, telling it that there is no reason to be concerned about what is happening because you were safe. This connection becomes damaged and stops sending communications. Your amygdala constantly tells you a threat is happening, and your prefrontal cortex cannot tell it to calm down.

In essence, you become the wounded nail, and everything around you is a hammer waiting to inflict more pain. This breaks down your ability to logically reason and listen to the literal words being told to you. Your amygdala tells you there is a hidden message in them that reinforces your fears that you are in danger.

That hidden message tells you that your worst fears are true. You are about to get in trouble, it’s your fault, you will be abandoned, or you are a burden to everyone around you. The constant alarm system of your amygdala inhibits your brain’s ability to calm or soothe you and tells you the trauma is happening again, or a new trauma is occurring.

If you think about when you have been in a building where a loud fire alarm is going off, it is hard to focus on anything around you or hear instructions. Your amygdala is that fire alarm in your brain that is constantly overriding any other information coming through.

Trauma teaches the brain that to stay safe, you must prioritize threat detection because the trauma has taught you that your ability to detect what is safe can no longer be trusted. Specifically, when your past has involved repeated danger, criticism, abuse, unpredictability, betrayal, or abandonment, your brain becomes exceptionally skilled at searching for signs that something bad is coming.

Interpretation of Communication

What this means is that everyday conversations or even the slightest hint of conflict will be examined as danger without being able to process the true meaning or words being said.

If your partner has a neutral facial expression, you will automatically interpret it as anger. Instead of them just thinking about something else. A delayed text means rejection. Instead of an interruption. A sigh is irritation or disapproval, meaning you’re a burden or it’s your fault, instead of them thinking about the long list of tasks still to do at work or that they didn’t sleep well.

Every little gesture, behavior, expression, or action is interpreted as if you are the cause or at fault. “Why did you say that?” is interpreted as “You’re a monster.” “I wish you would have done [something]” is heard as “It’s your fault this happened.”

Tone and body language become louder than the words being said. Tone is often misinterpreted as having an edge to it. Even when your partner says they are not angry, you interpret that as a lie because you’re hyper-focused on the tone and non-verbal cues. Your traumatized nervous system will say, “That’s a lie! They’re trying to trick me!”

You’ve become unable to consciously discern or translate any communication as positive because every communication subconsciously reinforces that you’re under attack. This is due to your nervous system constantly performing threat appraisal in everything you see or hear. Your amygdala is telling you that your threat responses are your only option. Your response must be fight, flight, freeze, or fawn (appeasing your attacker).

When your communication activates your trauma response, your ability to calmly process language diminishes. You can’t listen to understand the content or message. Your communication problems with your partner are an inability to regulate emotions/fear or understand the exact meaning of what is being said. That is, they are not failures in communication, but failures in regulation and threat assessment. You have damaged filters.

Trauma Threat Responses

Instead, your nervous system is telling you to go into survival mode, or you won’t make it. In communication, this can occur in one or more of the following ways:

Fight: arguing, defensiveness, anger, disruption, counterattacking.

Flight: leaving the conversation, deflecting, changing the subject, avoiding texts or calls.

Freeze: going blank, becoming silent, dissociating, being unable to answer, shutting down.

Fawn: immediately agreeing, apologizing, appeasing, or saying what the other person wants to hear – even if you disagree [anything to make it stop].

In healthy communication, we listen for meaning without bias. Trauma causes us to listen for danger with extreme prejudice that everything has a hidden meaning and everyone has a hidden agenda. Instead of listening to the words your partner is saying you listen to why this means danger.

Your nervous system constantly asks: “Are they angry? Am I in trouble? Are they criticizing me? Are they going to leave? Am I losing control? Do I need to defend myself? What aren’t they telling me?”

The conclusions you automatically draw are: “I’ve done something wrong again. I’m a failure. They hate me. I can never do anything right. I’m useless. I’m worthless. Why bother? I must defend myself. I’m unsafe. I’m all alone. No one understands me. They would be better off without me.”

Once your internal threat monitor goes off, you lose the ability to clearly discern what is being said. Everything you hear from then on is filtered through your trauma and past negative experiences. It’s as if everyone from your past suddenly is standing behind your partner, shouting all the defeating and threatening thoughts your nervous system is interpreting.

Your ability to rationally listen to the content and truth is completely disconnected. It’s like someone has pulled the plug on your prefrontal cortex and pushed the gas pedal on your amygdala. All rational thought has left the building. Suddenly your present conversation becomes connected to, or just plain becomes, an old conversation that you have had with more than just your partner. All current meaning, issues, or problems are irrelevant.

The ability to solve the current issue or find any resolution flies out the window. When communicating involves heightened emotions, dredging up the past, or the inability to regulate emotions, it can be nearly impossible to find resolution. Then, when you are not only communicating with your partner but also with those from your past, conflict will only escalate, and a feeling of unsafety, as well as hopelessness for change, will set in.

Ambiguous Communication

Often communication becomes ambiguous, leaving a lot unsaid and open to interpretation. For a person who has not had trauma, that ambiguity is frequently left at face value, and nuances or motives are not read into it. For those with a history of trauma, that ambiguity becomes subject to a whole host of new dangers and threats.

If your partner texts you to “call when you get a chance,” a person without trauma will think, “Sure, as soon as I get a second.” However, for those with a history of trauma, it sends you into a catastrophic spiral that can lead to all kinds of dangerous conclusions.

For example, you will start thinking, “Something is wrong, I did something wrong, they’re angry with me, I’m about to be rejected, they hate me, I can’t do anything right, everything is my fault, they’re going to abandon me, I’m all alone.” It’s the same six words in a text that have completely different meanings for the person with no history of trauma than the nervous system response for the one with trauma.

Information that is incomplete means the brain has to fill in the missing pieces. Ambiguity means uncertainty, which means unpredictability that leads to danger and worst-case scenarios being played out over and over again in your thoughts.

Rejection, Abandonment, and Boundaries

A history of rejection or abandonment can also complicate how communication is received in the same way that ambiguity does. In communication and relationships, boundaries are essential and healthy. However, to those with rejection or abandonment issues, boundaries mean they are about to relive that all over again.

Setting a healthy boundary before conflict is discussed increases the likelihood of calmer discussions and ultimate resolution. Yet to the person with trauma those healthy boundaries, such as “I can’t talk about this now” or “I need space” or “We’ll talk later.” These boundaries are interpreted as “You’re trying to control me” or “You’re rejecting me” or “You’re leaving me.”

This can produce pursuit, anxious attachment, reassurance seeking, anger, withdrawal, or attempts to control the conversation, which may ironically create the very relational distance the person fears. Trauma-induced catastrophic thinking then creates confirmation loops based on beliefs or stuck points that come from the trauma.

Trauma and Memory

In addition, trauma can also affect memory during conversations due to the nervous system being heightened. When your amygdala has sent out the threat signal, your emotions go into overdrive. The prefrontal cortex goes offline, resulting in every word being heard through emotions and shame. When you are in a heightened emotional state, you have a difficult time storing logical, organized, consecutive memories.

High arousal can interfere with attention, working memory, organization, and encoding of information. Someone may leave a difficult conversation remembering only fragments, especially the most emotionally threatening pieces. Two people can therefore walk away with strikingly different memories of the same discussion.

This doesn’t mean that neither party was listening. It means that neither party was hearing the same conversation. The trauma-affected brain prioritizes information in association with what is necessary for survival rather than context.

Furthermore, a common coping mechanism that results from trauma is dissociation. This happens to separate the victim from the trauma to protect them from what is happening. This becomes a response the brain becomes attached to and fond of. If I separate my conscious mind from what is happening around me, I don’t have to experience what is happening, and then I don’t have to relive it later.

Dissociation can become such an unhealthy coping mechanism that the slightest hint of conflict, stress, triggers, or danger can result in being mentally checked out from reality. If the brain is off in another world, memories of what is currently occurring cannot be stored. If I’m not aware of what is happening, I can believe I am safe.

Dissociation can start occurring so frequently that you become less in touch with reality and start to isolate yourself in your own mental world. To your partner, you may appear calm and listening while internally you are detached, numb, foggy, or mentally absent.

You may nod and respond in short statements, like “okay,” but will later have no recollection that the conversation took place. You appear to be compliant and agreeable. However, compliance is not necessarily comprehension. Silence is not listening, and your calm appearance is not you being in control of your emotions.

The Need for Control

Trauma that involves a state of helplessness creates a powerful need for predictability and control. One of the main symptoms or effects of this type of trauma is a need for control in every aspect of your life. “If I am in control, I am safe, and trauma cannot happen to me again. If I am not in control, I am at risk and in danger.”

The need for control starts impacting every area of your life, including your communication. During conversations, this can appear as needing an immediate answer, demanding certainty, repeatedly asking the same question, controlling when or how discussions occur, struggling when someone needs space, or becoming distressed when outcomes remain unresolved.

This also leads to requests or conflict being interpreted as “they’re trying to control me. If I am being controlled, I am going to be hurt again.”

Why Better Communication and Listening Aren’t Always Enough

Now that you are aware of how your nervous system disrupts your ability to receive what is being said, how do we make communication clearer? Traditionally, advice on communication asserts that appropriate words should be chosen, like using “I” statements, not interrupting, listening actively – not being focused on your response while your partner is talking, paraphrasing, and avoiding blame.

However, when your communication has been hijacked by your nervous system and past trauma, these important skills won’t matter. Your nervous system is actively trying to discern how big the threat is, how much danger you are in, and telling you the worst-case scenario is going to happen.

Remember the amygdala and prefrontal cortex? Trauma has broken the ability for those primary parts of your brain to communicate with each other. It has also increased the size of your amygdala, which is constantly on alert and sends signals that a looming threat is in every conversation, facial expression, body language, and tone. With your nervous system being alert, you will not be able to focus on the normal pathways for healthy communication.

So, what do you need to do? Is your communication doomed to misconceptions forever? Not at all! However, there are steps that need to be taken before you can start directly addressing how you perceive communication. You see, when your emotions are dysregulated or unstable, you can’t just choose to control them.

Emotional Regulation

You need to be able to get your emotions regulated and start processing the misconceptions or stuck points you have surrounding your trauma before you will be able to hear the content that is being spoken. This takes therapy.

When someone experiences trauma, one of the most common symptoms that comes from it is avoidance. This is a common problem among most trauma survivors. It is also one of the most dangerous behaviors that inhibits your trauma recovery.

When trauma is avoided, it does not go away. It festers just like an infection and starts to invade every area of your life. This process of festering does not have a specific timeline. For some, it will spread quickly after the trauma, impairing your ability to function. Then you learn how to avoid it, and you become a master at that avoidance. You convince yourself you’ve moved on and the trauma isn’t affecting you.

You tell everyone you are good at compartmentalizing it. It doesn’t bother you. The problem is, like any compartment, it can only hold so much. Initially, it will start by leaking. You develop maladaptive behaviors: overeating, addictions, isolation, too much spending, anger outbursts, etc. You are in denial that there is a trauma root to your behavior.

These maladaptive behaviors start interrupting your relationships, causing issues at work, your anger starts growing, or you are easily overwhelmed at the slightest task. You will slack at work, be constantly late, and call out more frequently. You might start to overreact to situations that are minor and underreact to situations that should be concerning because you don’t care what happens to you.

Eventually the compartment gets too full, and it bursts open. Your relationships start to crumble, your job is at risk – if not lost, your world gets smaller the more you withdraw and isolate. Conflict increases and communication crumbles. Anger and emotions are out of control. You and your family are left wondering what is wrong.

Regulation must happen before resolution can. Recovery through therapy starts with education about what is going on. You may feel like you are crazy, but you’re not. You have been wounded, and it hasn’t been able to heal. Each time you have avoided it, that avoidance has fed it, causing it to grow. Now it is so big it can no longer be avoided. It is time to start processing it, but it doesn’t mean you have to relive it.

Addressing Feelings

You must address how it has made you feel, and the stuck points or misconceptions you have created surrounding it, such as believing it is your fault. Your need for control of everything has gotten to a point of exhaustion.

By working through these stuck points and stopping the constant analysis paralysis of the event, trying to make it more acceptable or understandable as to why it happened. You find that the only thing you have some control over is blaming yourself. If you were responsible, then you could prevent it from happening again.

While you start learning how your trauma has affected you, your partner also needs to be educated on what is going on. Additionally, if your partner has trauma, it adds even more complications to your communication. You each are filtering what is said through your own trauma. Awareness and knowledge provide reassurance and safety that have long been missing.

As awareness increases, as well as your ability to recognize safety, you become more able to regulate your emotions. When your emotions calm down, it means your nervous system starts taking a break. You become more able to feel connection to the ones you love. Then your communication can start improving, and you are better able to solve problems because your prefrontal cortex is brought back online.

Education and knowledge provide a chance for trauma-informed communication. When you and your partner know the barriers and how you each interpret what is being said, you become more prepared to improve your communication.

Trauma-Informed Communication

Trauma-informed communication can involve slowing the interaction, decreasing intensity, using clear rather than ambiguous language, avoiding unnecessary ultimatums, checking what the person heard rather than assuming understanding, allowing processing time, validating emotions without necessarily agreeing with interpretations, maintaining predictable boundaries, and returning to difficult conversations after regulation has been restored.

The most important part of restoring communication is separating emotions from it. If you are angry, emotional, or struggling to control your emotions, do not engage in conflict or try to have conversations about problems if you cannot keep your emotions out of it. When you are emotional, your amygdala is rapidly firing, warning of danger.

This is where boundaries are important. You must establish a period where you can calm down and rationally talk about the problems at hand. You cannot find resolution if you cannot communicate. Once you can calmly discuss the situation, you need to stay on the task at hand. Do not bring up past issues.

As you talk, keep checking in on your emotions and do grounding techniques (breathing exercises, count backwards, things that keep you present and calm). Your nervous system cannot send your amygdala into overdrive if you are trying to solve problems like counting backwards; your prefrontal cortex has to be fully engaged.

As things your partner says start to trigger those feelings of being blamed or things filtered through shame, it is time to clarify. Tell your partner, “This is what I heard you say. Is that what you meant?” These questions can quickly provide clarification for misconceptions and close the gap in communication.

Tell your partner how what they said triggered your feelings and discuss between the two of you what is triggering and find other ways that thoughts might be expressed. When you and your partner can educate each other about the intent behind what is being said, feelings can be expressed, and resolution can occur. Knowing the intent behind a conversation can lead to a greater understanding instead of misunderstanding.

We don’t receive communication with our ears alone. We hear it through the filter of everything we have survived, learned, feared, and come to expect. Sometimes our history is listening too.

item.title: Therapy for Parenting Adult Children: Have You Actually Let Go?
item.description:
You pride yourself on allowing your adult children to live their own lives. You may even counsel other parents on how to do the same when their children reach the age of maturity. “Don’t interfere!” you correct. “They’re adults,” you say. You might even share examples of how you have allowed your adult children, with God’s guidance, to make all their own choices.

While it’s wonderful that you feel good in your role as a parent, has it ever occurred to you that you haven’t actually let go, but have just changed the way you hold on?

Many parents create distance with their children once they reach adulthood. And the reasons vary. Some parents might be pure in motive and mature in execution of their new relationship dynamics. But for some families, there can be a tremendous upheaval in dynamics and intimacy between a parent and their child on the cusp of adulthood.

Obviously, parenting doesn’t end on your child’s eighteenth birthday, but it does have to shift, and authority has to change. The proximity might also change, but the heart must change too, and often, that’s the hardest part.

Letting Go is Not the Same as Withdrawing

Many parents get confused by the idea of letting go of their children and emotional distance. They think that stepping back means giving less advice or pretending not to notice when their adult children are struggling. But biblically speaking, love isn’t cold detachment. In fact, it’s the opposite.

Scriptures tell us that we must love deeply, wisely, and without being controlling. So, letting go means releasing authority over your children, not the love for them with it. And those two things are significantly different.

When Their Problems Become Your Problems

When you see your adult child overwhelmed due to their sketchy finances or their marriage is strained, it can feel as if it were your own problem. Maybe even more intensely. Their problem becomes your problem.

Is this love? Or could it be anxiety?

If what you’re feeling is simply love for your child, then you will respond that you care deeply for what they’re going through. You will be empathetic and caring.

But if anxiety is in the mix, then your brain will start to scan for ways to fix the problem, rather than love them through a solution.

When your emotional state rises and falls right along with your adult child’s circumstances, something important happens internally. While you might not be meddling outwardly, inwardly, you’re still tightly gripping their hand.

Emotional Over-Involvement

Sometimes what looks like deep parental love to the outside world is actually a case of blurred emotional boundaries. Signs of this might include feeling responsible for regulating their emotions, a belief that their struggles are a reflection of your failures in parenting, or panic when they don’t follow your advice.

Pure compassion and love allow you to sit beside your children, being a listening ear, and being practically active in their lives when invited. But emotional over-involvement can cause you to feel responsible for eliminating those problems rather than helping them through them. If this is the case with you and your adult children, you might be dealing with attachment wounds or unresolved fears in your own life.

Attachment Doesn’t Expire on Their Eighteenth Birthday

Attachment theory can help explain why this transition of watching your child turn into an adult can be emotionally confusing and destabilizing.

If you have an anxious attachment pattern, you are likely to feel the safest when you’re indispensable. After all, you’ve been your child’s protector, provider, and guide for the better part of two decades.

When your child struggled, it activated your protector instinct, but it also reinforced your role as necessary. Their need became a form of reassurance to you of your importance. That type of attachment doesn’t just disappear overnight.

If you lean more avoidant, you might actually swing in the opposite direction. You might tell yourself that your child made their choices and they must suffer whatever natural consequence comes. While this might sound strong and like good parenting, it might also be a sign of emotional distance that complicates the connection with your adult child.

The Fine Line Between Intervention and Meddling

As your child transitions from childhood to adulthood, one of the trickiest areas to traverse is knowing when to step in and when to step back. While they look eerily similar, the key difference comes down to your motivation.

Intervention is guided by love and your unique body of wisdom that includes life experience and your immense understanding of them as a person. Intervention often includes observing a harmful pattern and then speaking up, gently and respectfully, as one adult to another.

It can also manifest as offering a perspective once, and with deep humility, and then trusting God with the outcome.

Meddling is vastly different; it is driven by fear, control, or unresolved attachment needs, not purely love. This comes out in real life as repeating advice until your adult child finally complies or pressuring them to make a decision that matches your expectations rather than your own.

One of the significant differences between meddling and intervention also comes down to whether you’re honoring their adulthood. You are no longer their authority figure, and intervention honors that. It places you solidly into the role you’re supposed to be in at this stage in life. You become their supporter, mentor, and prayer partner instead of their fixer.

When Will They Learn to Stand in Their Own Consequences

Experiencing consequences, whether that’s financial, relational, or any other way, is the primary way that people learn responsibility and gain wisdom. As tempting as it may be to step into your adult child’s circumstances and cushion the fall, overprotecting them, even at this stage, can stunt their growth. Even more detrimental than that is that it can also delay them in learning the lessons that God intends for them to learn.

Of course, there are times when you should step in, but before you do, ask yourself if you are doing so because the situation is truly dangerous or if you’re stepping in to relieve yourself of the discomfort of watching them struggle. If it’s the latter, you may be trying to cure your own anxiety and quiet your own fear, rather than demonstrating love for them.

The Art of Letting Go (And Letting God)

You’ve probably heard the statement, “Let go and let God,” a hundred times. While that simple statement can oversimplify real life, there is a truth behind the words.

Trusting God’s work in their life is really what your job as a parent has been all along. When they were little, of course, you had to guide them and protect them in practical ways, but you also showed them how God showed up in their circumstances and yours.

That guidance doesn’t have to stop. You can still share the ways that God has shown up for you in your life. You can still point out God’s provision, protection, and possible correction, even into their adult years. But your involvement must wane as they take stewardship and ownership of their own lives.

Struggling with Letting Go?

Therapy can help you identify patterns of emotional over-involvement as well as unresolved attachment wounds or anxiety-driven behaviors that might be making letting go difficult.

Therapy can provide you with a place to explore your fears, and whether they’re rooted in reality or trauma. Or maybe you will discover that they are a reflection of your own lack of faith in Christ. You can also learn to develop practical strategies for setting healthy, adult-friendly boundaries.

Separating your own emotions and identity from your child’s choices and learning how to intervene properly rather than meddle can not only relieve you of guilt and the weight of responsibility but can also enhance or even repair your relationship with your adult child.

If you’re struggling with your role as the parent of an adult, contact our office to meet with one of the therapists in our network for a one-on-one session where you can explore these complex and destabilizing factors in this season of life.

item.title: What Most Women Wish Someone Had Told Them About Menopause and Depression
item.description:
Menopause is one of those life stages that everyone knows is coming, yet few women feel truly prepared for. Conversation about it is often limited to hot flashes, night sweats, or the end of monthly cycles. What is rarely discussed in detail is the emotional impact, especially the connection between menopause and depression.

Many women discover this reality only once they are living through it. They may wake up one morning feeling unusually sad, irritable, or disconnected, and wonder why. Some describe it as a fog that settles over their daily life. Others notice that tasks they once handled with ease suddenly feel draining. Because the emotional side of menopause is not openly discussed, women often feel blindsided when depression becomes part of their experience.

The silence regarding menopause and depression is one of the biggest challenges. Women are told to expect physical changes, but the emotional toll is minimized. This lack of open conversation leaves many feeling isolated, unsure whether what they are experiencing is normal, and uncertain where to turn for help.

One of the biggest challenges is that younger women grow up with a lot of myths about menopause.

Myths Younger Women Believe About Menopause

  • Some believe it happens overnight, as if one day periods stop and everything changes instantly.
  • Others think menopause is only about hot flashes or that depression during this stage is simply moodiness.
  • There is also a myth that menopause is the same for everyone. Younger women may assume that all women experience the same symptoms in the same way. This belief can make it harder to accept the wide range of experiences that exist.
  • Another common myth is that menopause only affects women in their late fifties. Often, symptoms begin much earlier. Some women notice changes in their forties, and others even sooner.

Depression linked to hormonal shifts can appear long before the final menstrual cycle. These myths create confusion and make it harder for women to recognize what is really happening when the time comes.

When Menopause Really Begins

Menopause is not a single event. It is a process, and the first stage is called perimenopause. This transition can last several years. During perimenopause, hormone levels fluctuate, cycles become irregular, and emotional changes begin to surface.

Perimenopause is not very well known because women may still have their periods, leading them to believe menopause has not started. Yet this stage is when many symptoms of menopause and depression first appear. Sleep disturbances, sudden irritability, and unexplained sadness are common.

Awareness that perimenopause is part of the journey is a way to help women understand that depression during this time is not unusual.

Perimenopause also highlights how gradual the process can be. Some women experience subtle changes that build slowly, while others face sudden shifts that feel disruptive. Understanding this stage helps women prepare for what lies ahead rather than being caught off guard.

How Menopause Manifests Differently in Women

One of the least discussed realities is how differently menopause manifests in women. Some experience mostly physical symptoms, such as hot flashes, night sweats, or weight changes. Others find the emotional side more challenging, with depression, anxiety, or loss of motivation taking center stage.

There is no single pattern. A woman may feel fine physically but struggle emotionally. Another may have intense physical discomfort but little depression. This variation is why menopause and depression are hard to generalize. Each woman’s experience is unique, shaped by genetics, lifestyle, and personal history.

Even within families, experiences can differ. Mothers or sisters may go through menopause at different ages with very different symptoms. This diversity is rarely acknowledged, leaving women to wonder why their experience does not match what they have heard from others.

Why Menopause and Depression Are Not Well Understood

Menopause and depression remain poorly understood for several reasons. First, medical training often focuses more on reproductive health than on the emotional impact of menopause. Many doctors are not fully equipped to explain the mental health side of this transition.

Second, cultural silence plays a role. In many communities, menopause is treated as something private, not openly discussed. Women may feel embarrassed to talk about depression or mood changes, fearing judgment or dismissal.

Third, research into menopause and depression has historically been limited compared to other health issues. This lack of attention means fewer resources and less public awareness. As a result, women are left searching for answers on their own.

Finally, the overlap between menopause symptoms and other life stressors adds to the confusion. Women in midlife may be balancing careers, divorce, caring for children, or supporting aging parents. Depression during menopause may be dismissed as general stress, when in fact hormonal changes are playing a significant role.

The Everyday Struggles No One Talks About

Menopause and depression affect daily life in ways that are rarely acknowledged. Concentration at work may become harder. Tasks that once felt simple, like cooking dinner or managing schedules, may feel draining. In addition, relationships can be strained when mood changes are misunderstood.

Sleep problems are another everyday struggle. Night sweats and insomnia leave women exhausted, which worsens depression. Fatigue makes it harder to cope with stress, creating a cycle that feels difficult to break.

Social connections may also suffer. Women sometimes withdraw from friends or family because they feel misunderstood. This isolation deepens depression and makes the transition even harder.

While menopause and depression bring challenges, there are practical ways to find support. Women do not have to face this stage alone.

Practical Ways to Seek Real Day‑to‑Day Support

Steps to consider include:

  • Track symptoms. Keeping a journal of mood changes, sleep patterns, and physical symptoms can help identify triggers and patterns.
  • Focus on lifestyle habits. Regular exercise, balanced nutrition, and consistent sleep routines can ease both physical and emotional symptoms.
  • Communicate with family and friends. Explaining what menopause and depression feel like helps loved ones provide better support.
  • Join support groups. Many communities and online platforms offer spaces where women share experiences and advice. Hearing others’ stories can reduce feelings of isolation.
  • Talk to a healthcare professional who understands menopause and depression. Ask specific questions about emotional symptoms, not just physical ones.
  • Explore counseling or therapy. Mental health professionals can provide coping strategies and help women process the emotional side of menopause.

These practical steps make the journey more manageable and remind women that support is available.

Menopause and depression are realities many women wish someone had explained earlier. The silence around emotional symptoms leaves women unprepared, while myths and misunderstandings add confusion.

Acknowledging important precursory stages (like perimenopause), understanding the differences in how menopause manifests, and having some insight into why these issues are not well explained are all part of building awareness.

The everyday struggles of menopause and depression are real, but so are the ways to find help. Professionally guided support groups across the USA, as well as one‑on‑one counseling, offer safe spaces to learn, prepare, and cope.

Seeking guidance even before menopause or perimenopause begins can help women feel knowledgeable and ready for the unknown symptoms ahead. If you are considering support, know that help is available. Reach out to a professional today to begin preparing for this stage of life with confidence and care.

If you need more information or would like to get started with pre-menopause counseling, there are numbers on this site you can call. Contact us today to learn more.

item.title: Can Emotionally-Focused Couples Therapy Save Your Marriage After an Affair?
item.description:
Everything you thought you knew about your marriage changes when there has been an affair. The questions are tougher to answer, and the closeness becomes an afterthought. It is a rawness that asks if it can be survived.

For some couples, the answer is an honest and painful no. But for others, there is another route to take. It is the route where the yes leads to emotionally focused couples therapy (EFCT). This type of therapy leads to understanding of what happened, identifying the needs of each spouse, and rebuilding a marriage after honest evaluation from both spouses.

What Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy Is — and What It Isn’t

Emotionally focused couples therapy was developed in the 80s and grounded in attachment theory. Science emphasizes how people bond and what repair requires. The idea is that humans are wired for close bonds, and when those bonds break down, people act out. Anger and withdrawal aren’t indications of bad behavior. They are misguided attempts at connection that have gone wrong. When you and your spouse recognize this distinction, it changes everything about how healing begins.

The conversation then shifts from how this happens towards something that is more useful but harder. This conversation revolves around what was really happening between you and what each of you will need to do going forward. Emotionally focused couples therapy is effective at preventing relapse only when both spouses engage with genuine honesty. There has to be a mutual willingness to go through the process in order to reach the desired results.

Some Christian counselors are trained to assist Christian couples in finding a connection of faith and a therapeutic process to heal and move forward after an affair. The counselor can help couples understand the positive intent underneath even the most negative behavior.

Why It Feels Like More Than Heartbreak?

The affair breaks trust, and underneath that lies an emotional bond that was already becoming frayed. Through EFCT, the Christian counselor and both spouses pursue the bond and not just the behavior. If you are the betrayed spouse, then what you feel goes beyond hurt and rejection.

Infidelity produces trauma-like symptoms, such as insomnia, flashbacks, intrusive thoughts, and hypervigilance about feeling safe. These symptoms are not an overreaction. This is the response of your nervous system to a profound wound. Emotionally focused couples therapy treats this for what it is without rushing you toward forgiveness until the injury has been fully acknowledged.

Infidelity will also produce symptoms in the individual who initiated the affair. Shame, regret, and disconnection become the weight that a spouse will carry after they have been unfaithful. EFCT will also help with this.

Regardless of which side you are on, there is no justifying what happened, but both experiences need to be understood before healing can take place. Scripture teaches us to bear one another’s burdens not because it is easy, but because that is what genuine love and commitment look like when they are tested.

When a couple can engage honestly with the process, they will find improvements in intimacy and forgiveness over time. EFCT allows the couple to sit in the hard moments of this engagement. By sitting in these moments, the couple starts to reach for each other again instead of defending themselves. It is this shift in the relationship that EFCT builds toward.

What Makes Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy Different?

Not every form of therapy is built to handle the damage that an affair causes. An affair is an attachment injury, and not just a communication problem. Attachment injury requires care that reaches deeper than communication, coaching, or conflict resolution strategies.

This distinction is important in choosing the correct approach that will help a couple who has faced infidelity. Emotionally focused couples therapy focuses on a different premise entirely.

Even the most successful therapy model for highly distressed couples is not as effective as EFCT. Couples whose trust had been destroyed by an affair were able to heal through this process. Christian counselors trained in EFCT are able to bring clinical expertise together with a faith-based understanding of the covenant and focus on the genuine human capacity for change.

Infidelity healing requires that both partners open up and talk about the pain honestly. It means they have to have the hard conversation about what led to the affair without assigning blame. The conversation leads the way to understanding so that an effective apology can be given. It is also vital to have an effective acknowledgment of the apology. Each person in the relationship is part of this conversation.

What Does the Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy Look Like?

Infidelity healing through emotionally focused couples therapy is slow, challenging, and rarely in a straight line. In the beginning, the sessions focus on building enough safety for both spouses to be honest about the emotional patterns that existed prior to infidelity. Conversation about the affair is not part of these early sessions, but rather it is about the patterns that were underneath it.

Typically, the therapist will help you and your spouse identify and interrupt negative cycles that the marriage has been locked into. The cycles of pursuing and withdrawing, and shutting down and blaming, are replaced by patterns that are more sustainable. The unfaithful spouse takes accountability without defensiveness, and the injured spouse is required to stay present with the pain and not use it as a permanent wall.

Not every marriage will make it; sometimes, one or both spouses decide the damage is too much. But even then, therapy can make it possible to end things without heavy fallout. For those couples who choose to stay with the process, they will build something more honest than what they had before. The old relationship will be gone, and something new will be built.

What does Scripture say about this kind of bearing with each other? Colossians emphasizes patience, compassion, and bearing with one another even when it costs something. Christian counselors who specialize in this field understand that the goal isn’t just restoring things to their original state, but rather achieving something even better.

What Does the Process Ask of Each Spouse?

There is no straight line to healing through emotionally focused couples therapy, and the early sessions don’t focus on the affair. Through honesty about the emotional patterns that existed before infidelity, safety can be built to ensure healing conversations. Christian counselors are able to help identify and interrupt the negative cycles that once consumed the relationship.

Navigating this process means honesty and accountability from both sides. EFCT requires that each spouse move out of the mindset of pointing blame, becoming defensive, or shutting down. It will require that you and your spouse navigate the process with compassion and patience, regardless of what it will cost in the moment.

Christian counselors are able to help with infidelity recovery by emphasizing that the goal is to build something more honest and more resilient, rather than trying to restore what was lost. Sometimes, couples find that the damage is too serious, and the marriage doesn’t survive. For the couples who choose to work hard and stay with it, they will find that they can rebuild with purpose.

Could EFCT Help Your Relationship?

It is important that you and your spouse reach out for help as soon as possible. The reality is that by waiting for the pain to fade or for an honest conversation to be enough, the negative cycles become stronger. By choosing emotionally focused couples therapy, you are choosing a proactive investment in your future with your spouse. However, it only works if both of you are willing to engage honestly.

It doesn’t matter when the affair came to light; what matters is that there’s no wrong time to begin EFCT. For more information or to schedule an appointment with a counselor, contact our office today and speak with our reception team. They will be happy to answer questions and provide you with information to choose to rebuild the marriage that infidelity damaged.

The work ahead won’t be easy, but when you and your spouse are willing, the investment can pay off with a stronger marriage.

item.title: Treatment and Recovery Options for Different Types of Eating Disorders
item.description:
Eating disorders are a reality many Americans have to deal with, affecting people of all walks of life, age, race, or gender. Every year in the US, around 10,000 precious lives are lost as a direct result of an eating disorder. Nearly thirty million people in the US will struggle with an eating disorder during their lifetime. Eating disorders are becoming even more prevalent among young adults and adolescents.

With disordered eating affecting so many people, not just in the US, but across the world, knowing what they are and how to best support a loved one with an eating disorder is that much more important. For those struggling with eating disorders, understanding what they’re going through can help them process the experience. It can also help them find ways to move toward wholeness and feeling healthy.

Eating Disorders: Understanding What They Are

There are many ideas out there about what eating disorders are, how they affect a person, and who is affected. It may be helpful, by way of naming the myths surrounding eating disorders, to clarify what eating disorders are. One myth about them is that having an eating disorder is a choice that a person makes. The reality is that eating disorders are serious mental health conditions that are the result of complex causes.

Another myth that is abroad about eating disorders is that you can tell if someone has an eating disorder just by looking at them. There is, supposedly, a ‘look’ that a person with an eating disorder has, but this is based on some truth and the power of popular media. The reality is that many people who are struggling with an eating disorder will fall within the average or typical weight range, or they may appear healthy. It isn’t always easy to tell.

The other myth that is out there is that only or mainly teenage girls are the ones who get eating disorders. However, the truth is that people of all walks of life, genders, ages, and cultural backgrounds are affected by eating disorders.

These myths can make it harder to recognize problems, and people may delay seeking appropriate treatment. If you have an eating disorder, but one or more of these myths affect your perception or the perception of the people around you, your struggles may get dismissed or minimized. That can lead to a worsening of the problem.

Eating disorders are mental health conditions that go beyond any social or class divide. To address them, they need to be recognized for what they are, and professional help sought. A counselor can nurture the physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual well-being of the individual affected by them.

The Different Types of Eating Disorders

There are several types of eating disorders that have been identified and categorized over the years. They each have particular defining features that differentiate them, and their symptoms will also look different.

  • Bulimia Nervosa: This eating disorder involves a person getting caught up in cycles of binge eating that are followed by compensatory behaviors such as vomiting, fasting, using laxatives, or doing excessive exercise to deal with the excess consumption and get rid of extra calories. A person who suffers from bulimia will often feel that they have a lack of control during their episodes of binging.
  • Typically, after binge-eating, the episode is accompanied by feelings of shame and guilt.
  • Anorexia Nervosa: Often simply referred to as anorexia, this eating disorder is characterized by a person adhering to an extreme restriction on their food intake. Likewise, they have an intense fear of gaining weight and a distorted body image. Even if they have lost weight and are underweight or malnourished, they might continue to consider themselves overweight and carry on restricting what they eat.An individual with anorexia may also exhibit excessive exercise habits and be in denial of the severity of their condition.
  • Binge-Eating Disorder: This disorder is characterized by recurring episodes of eating large quantities of food, often rapidly and to the point of discomfort, without regular use of compensatory behaviors. This can lead to significant emotional distress and various health complications. Binge-eating may be triggered by stress or other emotional states such as sadness or feeling overwhelmed.One of the differences between binge-eating disorder and bulimia is that with binge-eating disorder, instead of taking the extreme measures one does with bulimia, one may use compensatory behaviors such as eating less food at mealtimes or dieting.
  • Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID): This eating disorder, which has been recently identified, is a feeding or eating disorder that is more common in children and young adolescents than older people. With ARFID, the individual significantly limits the quantity or variety of the food they consume. One impact of this is that it can cause malnutrition, significant weight loss, or psychosocial problems.
  • Other Specified Feeding and Eating Disorders (OSFED): This category of eating disorders includes patterns of disordered eating that do not meet the exact criteria of the above disorders, but are nonetheless serious enough to impact emotional, mental, and physical wellbeing.

Key Signs of Eating Disorders

Eating disorders don’t all look or operate in the same way. The symptoms of each will be different. Each individual will have symptoms that are present in particular ways. Look out for a preoccupation with one’s body image or with food and dieting. This may be excessive, taking over a person’s life and attention.

Eating disorders can be signaled by a dramatic and noticeable weight loss or gain. Similarly, be concerned with conspicuous changes in eating habits such as eating secretively or skipping meals. If a person withdraws socially, especially from activities that involve food, take note. Gastrointestinal issues, irregular heart rhythms, or dizziness are linked to eating too much or too little.

You can also be on the lookout for hypersensitivity to food textures or taste, an aversion toward eating, and a fear of trying new foods. Should you encounter these concerns, it’s important to speak with a health professional for appropriate assessments and diagnosis. Some of the behaviors and symptoms associated with eating disorders may be linked to hormonal imbalances or life stressors, and a professional can help you discern this.

Treatment and Recovery Options for Eating Disorders

If you have a loved one with an eating disorder, how can you best support them? Educating yourself about the disorder they struggle with can help you to reduce your misconceptions and possible frustrations with your loved one. Being a present, non-judgmental presence makes a difference, as does creating a safe environment for your loved one to wrestle with and address the issues.

You can also offer your loved one acceptance and unconditional love. This doesn’t mean being blind to the issues but rather loving them in spite of it all. Choose to show up for them. Support them by encouraging them to seek and continue treatment from a professional. You can also pray for your loved ones, for comfort and strength.

Eating disorders indicate that a person may have an unhealthy relationship with food and their body. With the right support and effective treatment, it’s possible to attain goals such as rebuilding self-esteem, getting to a healthy body weight, and nurturing a healthy body image. It’s possible to begin noticing circumstances or situations that function as triggers for the eating disorder.

For effective treatment, several approaches may be necessary to achieve healing. A counselor will help by tailoring an approach that suits their client’s needs and addresses the situation effectively. A multidisciplinary approach may be necessary to effectively address an eating disorder. Immediate medical care may be necessary to see to physical health concerns from the eating disorder, for instance.

Apart from medical attention, guidance from dietitians and nutritionists is required to develop healthy eating patterns. There are support groups that can provide a sense of community and accountability as one struggles. Therapy may be helpful in pinpointing and addressing any underlying spiritual, emotional, and mental concerns that may be worsening the eating disorder.

When you are ready, you should reach out to a health professional to begin addressing any concerns you may have about eating disorders. Our office is available to receive your call and make an appointment with one of the Christian therapists in our practice. Begin your healing journey today!

item.title: Help for Single Moms (Older Mom Edition)
item.description:
When people hear about the struggles of the single mom, most think of the young mother juggling her new responsibilities of parenthood with the naivety of youth and maybe even the financial hardships most people face in their young adult lives. But not many people think of or acknowledge the unique struggles that some older moms face.

Perhaps society thinks that women, moms in particular, have life all figured out when they reach a certain age. Maybe they think that they don’t need the practical help they once did because their children are likely older and more self-sufficient.

But the reality that many people don’t understand is the hardship that can come from being an older single mother. Though, as an older mom, you aren’t as likely to be hand-feeding your children or having to hold their hands just to cross the street, you are facing some real and challenging obstacles.

Those Teenage Years

While the “terrible twos” get a lot of press in popular culture, parents of teens might argue that they are a piece of cake compared to the drama of a teenager. Hormones rage, bringing on physical changes in your child’s body and hot tempers you never knew lurked behind those innocent eyes.

Even two-parent households can struggle when their children reach their teens. Children at that age want to push their limits, explore independence, and learn what their true identity is apart from their parents. While there is nothing intrinsically wrong with this normal behavior, the “growing pains” can affect the single mom more than she is likely to admit.

Seeing your child grow into maturity is a beautiful experience, but seeing the comforts, security, and hopes of their childhood fade away is an emotionally daunting experience for parents. When a woman is alone during this time, she might feel particularly isolated, as her once-faithful little companion has grown into their own personhood and is often spending their time with friends or at activities rather than snuggling with mom.

In addition to potential loneliness, the weight of being the sole decision-maker in the household can be excruciating. “What time is curfew?” “When should I let them start dating?” “How do I talk to them about sex?”

These and a million other questions swirl through the single mother’s brain constantly, and without a partner to discuss them with, it can be overwhelming. With sole power also comes sole responsibility. A single mom knows that if she makes the wrong decisions for her child, she will feel responsible for the outcome.

Practical Help

As we age, our bodies no longer function quite the same way as they did in our youth. Mobility issues may intrude on performing everyday activities such as keeping the house clean or mowing the lawn. Without a partner in the house, a single mom might feel the effects of aging a little more harshly than someone who has a partner to take up the slack.

Some people think that mothers who have older children don’t have to worry about getting help with chores. They assume that the children will help fill in the gap where a father should stand. While it’s true that older children can more effectively clean up after themselves, do chores, and don’t need as much supervision, the reality is that the household workload still weighs mainly on mom’s shoulders.

Having children who, theoretically, can help and getting that practical help are two entirely different issues. Some older children have rigorous schedules of their own. Some play sports, participate in school activities such as theater or music, and have to keep up with their schoolwork. So even if the child is willing to help mom with household chores, the reality is that they often get left undone.

Some mothers try to deliberately limit the help they request from their older children. Typical age-appropriate chores are healthy for a child, but when the older child becomes a substitute parent for younger siblings, the weight of responsibility can be too much, and frankly unfair.

Assuming a mother of older children has fewer responsibilities than a mom of littles is unfair and probably untrue. As children get older, their needs shift, but don’t disappear.

Those busy schedules we just talked about? Mom is often the chauffeur of those events, particularly for kids who don’t have their own driver’s licenses. And any parent of active teens knows that they, too, will have a busy schedule.

There are games to cheer at, performances to attend, and other events that require a mother’s attendance. Children’s busy lives equal busy lives for parents, especially those doing it solo.

Facing Reality Alone

Along with all the practical responsibilities of single parenting comes the reality of doing life alone. When the kids are in bed, and mom is left to her own thoughts, it can be overwhelming to think about the reality of navigating life alone. Not just in this season, but in the next. And the next.

Loneliness is one thing, but the harsh reality of facing an empty nest that is truly empty, void of a partner or children, can be saddening and overwhelming.

The idea of growing old is daunting, too. It’s overwhelming for most people, even those with a partner, but growing old alone is a whole other world. “Will I be alone forever?” “Who will take care of me in my old age?”

These types of questions will haunt a single mom in still hours and create stress. Dreams of “growing old” with a partner may seem out of reach, and the reality that it might never actually happen can cause not only grief for unrealized dreams but anxiety about the future.

Therapy

One of the most helpful tools in a single mom’s toolbox is therapy. Therapy can help the older single mom on so many different levels. A therapist can step in to be that adult listening ear that is lacking in many single moms’ lives.

While it won’t replace the intimacy of a lifelong partner, a therapist can fulfill a similar, yet different, vital role. Your therapist can get to know you deeply and well and can help you make the decisions for yourself, your future, and your children that are weighing on your mind.

Most importantly, a Christian counselor can point you back to your loving Heavenly Father who has promised to be a father to the fatherless (By the way, that includes your children.) He also promises to be close to the widow (that includes you, no matter the reason you’re single).

Going to therapy, particularly with a Christian therapist, can also help you work through any trauma that might have happened that caused you to become a single mom in the first place. For some, it might be the trauma following the death of a spouse, for others, it’s the result of a divorce. There are many reasons a woman might find herself single-parenting, and a Christian therapist can help sort through the trauma and obstacles that got her there.

No One Said It Would Be Easy

No one ever said that single parenting would be easy, but for some reason, society thinks older moms need less help. As a single “older” mom, it’s your duty to inform those who hold this point of view.

Graciously share your heart with others who want to help. Accept any assistance you can from those in your ‘village’, whether that comes in the form of transportation for your child or the gift of a home-cooked meal.

And remember, when the going gets tough, the tough fall to their knees and pray for the wisdom and guidance of God. When you feel overwhelmed and alone, know that even though there isn’t a ring on your finger, you’re not parenting solo. You have God and professional therapists on your side.

To schedule an appointment with a professional Christian therapist, contact our office today.

item.title: When Family Wounds Run Deep: Understanding Moral Injury Between Siblings
item.description:
Sibling relationships are often thought of as one of the most enduring connections in our lives. It’s the connection with people who shared a childhood bedroom, a dinner table, and defining moments of growing up. But for many adults, this bond with a sibling carries something more complicated than nostalgia. The violation of deeply held values by a sibling causes serious harm and erodes the sense of safety that a family is meant to provide. The result is a wound described as moral injury.

This phenomenon goes deeper than a case of hurt feelings after a disagreement. Moral injury is the serious psychological damage that occurs when a person experiences something that fundamentally violates their moral framework. This type of wound in a sibling relationship can be disorienting as it strikes the core of family identity and belonging.

This type of pain requires compassionate attention, psychologically and spiritually. The complexity of these wounds rarely resolves without intentional support.

What Moral Injury Looks Like Between Siblings

The concept of moral injury gained recognition through research on veterans returning from combat. This was a framework for understanding what happens psychologically when people encounter events that violate their core beliefs of right and wrong. Mental health professionals are now recognizing that the same framework applies across a range of relationship settings, including the family.

This kind of wound between siblings can take many forms. It could come from a brother who stood by while abuse occurred or a sister who manipulated family resources and spread harmful lies that caused lasting damage to another’s reputation or life. It could have been a sibling who broke a sacred confidence shared in a moment of deep vulnerability. These offenses are not minor or ordinary family friction.

These are the events that alter the lens through which an injured person sees themselves, their family, and their place in the world. The damage lasts long after the event and involves the collapse of a trusted reality and a profound loss of the relationship. This kind of rupture in a family relationship deserves serious attention and should be handled with the care it requires.

For help, we can go to God. “The Lord is a stronghold for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble.” (Psalm 9:9, ESV) This reminds us of God’s faithfulness to us in even the hardest times of betrayal and mistrust.

The Hidden Weight Siblings Carry Alone

The most painful aspect of this situation is how invisible the hurt remains. Society has an expectation that can leave individuals who were harmed by a sibling feeling confused, ashamed, and as if their pain does not matter. Extended family or friends may offer advice during these moments, suggesting that the individual move on, but such responses can deepen the sense of isolation rather than ease it.

The individual who was harmed is trying to process the original event and grieve the relationship they believed they had. They are mourning the family they believed was the true version. This grief is heavy and complex and does not resolve quickly. What especially adds to difficulty is that sibling pain often lacks the social recognition that other losses receive.

There is no clear ritual for grieving a broken sibling bond, the way there is for other kinds of loss. This can leave a person feeling as though their pain is somehow invalid or excessive. It is important to recognize that individuals may need more than encouragement to forgive and to navigate this kind of deep pain. These individuals need an honest, supportive space to name what happened and understand what it has truly cost.

How Moral Injury Between Siblings Affects Mental Health

If the pain of sibling betrayal goes untreated, it will affect mental health significantly over time. Many individuals who carry these unresolved wounds may experience some symptoms that closely resemble Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.

People who experience moral injury could develop intrusive thoughts, emotional numbness, and a persistent sense of shame or self-blame related to the loss of a relationship due to an event that crossed a line. Some of these individuals may quietly question whether they deserve connection at all. In contrast, others develop deep patterns of distrust in their marriages, friendships, and even in their approaches to parenting.

Features of depression and anxiety can be common companions to this kind of loss. There is an unrelenting awareness that something fundamentally wrong happened and that people who should’ve cared did not. The result is an erosion of the person’s sense of worth and safety across many years.

Research in the field of relational trauma points to the fact that unresolved wounds from close family relationships can also surface in physical ways. These include disrupted sleep, chronic fatigue, and a diminished ability to regulate emotions in everyday situations. The body often holds what the mind has not yet fully processed.

Finding the proper support in these relational traumas will help in understanding the layered nature of this pain and offer care that addresses the emotional and spiritual dimensions of the pain the individual is facing. Connecting specifically with a Christian counselor can remind people how to come to Jesus as described in Matthew:

Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. – Matthew 11:28, ESV 

Navigating the Journey Toward Healing

Healing from this type of pain does not follow a straight line, nor does it always end in reconciliation. Some individuals find their journey toward wholeness means rebuilding a sense of personal identity damaged by betrayal. For others, it requires learning to grieve the lost relationship and the family they hoped for. Either way, the process asks something significant of the person who was hurt. It asks them to hold space for grief and growth at the same time, which is no small thing.

Christian counseling offers a structured and safe environment where those emotions can be worked through honestly without judgment. This type of counseling can also incorporate trauma-informed therapy, Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, and spiritually integrated counseling. Together, these approaches can help individuals work through complex relational pain.

The goal is to help individuals navigate moral injury by integrating their experience in ways that allow them to live more freely, form healthier connections, and discover a stable sense of self. Healing is the process that deserves skilled, compassionate, and constant support over time.

Hope for Healing

Sibling relationships are among the most formative in an individual’s life. When these relationships become a source of harm, the impact can linger for decades. Sibling betrayal pain is not something to dismiss or minimize. It is a serious form of psychological injury that touches areas of identity, faith, and sense of belonging.

No one should have to navigate that alone or carry the weight of a wound they were never meant to carry. Many people carry it silently for years, or sometimes decades. They move through life wondering why certain relationships feel impossible or why trust never quite settles. The connection between those patterns and an old sibling wound is often the last thing they consider examining.

Healing begins with honest acknowledgment supported by professional care and grounded in the truth that God does not abandon people in the depths of their pain. Reaching out for help regarding the aftermath of sibling betrayal is a meaningful and courageous act of self-respect. It is a step toward cultivating the wholeness you deserve.

If you are facing difficulty with pain related to moral injury from a sibling, reach out to a Christian counselor who understands the complexity of family pain to get you started on your way to healing.
